sections.title: Name and classification
sections.text: Hortiboletus rubellus (Krombh.) Simonini, Vizzini & Gelardi is a bolete in the family Boletaceae. First described as Boletus rubellus in 1836, it was transferred to Hortiboletus in 2015 following molecular work. Older literature may use Boletus rubellus or Xerocomellus rubellus.

sections.title: Description
sections.text: This rather small bolete has a convex cap that later expands, usually bright red to ruby red and sometimes fading with age. Its dry surface is finely velvety or tomentose; it often remains smooth but may crack in dry weather or near the margin. The tubes and pores are yellow, becoming olive-yellow to greenish; the angular pores slowly bruise blue when pressed. The flesh is pale to light yellow and may blue after cutting, with a variable reaction.

sections.title: Stem and habitat
sections.text: The stem is generally slender, yellow at the apex and reddish or red-streaked lower down, without a reticulate network. The flesh at the base may show tiny orange to vermilion-red dots, but this character varies and is also found in Hortiboletus engelii; it is not sufficient for identification. The species is ectomycorrhizal and occurs with various broadleaved trees — including oaks and beeches — in open woods, parks, gardens and other grassy, human-modified places.

sections.title: Lookalikes and edibility
sections.text: Cap colour and yellow pores alone do not reliably distinguish it from other reddish boletes, especially Hortiboletus engelii. Identification may require examining the stem base, microscopic characters, habitat and sometimes molecular data. The DGfM 2026 positive list includes H. rubellus among species considered edible after adequate cooking; that listing cannot identify a specimen and is not consumption advice.

traits: Cap usually ruby to bright red, convex then expanding; dry finely velvety surface, sometimes cracked in dry weather
Yellow tubes and pores becoming olive-yellow; angular pores slowly bruise blue when pressed
Slender stem, yellow at the apex and often reddish or red-streaked lower down; not reticulate
Tiny orange-red dots may occur in the stem-base flesh, but this variable character is shared with H. engelii
Ectomycorrhizal bolete with broadleaved trees, often in parks, gardens and open woods
safetyNote: The DGfM includes this species in its positive list subject to adequate cooking; an entry and photograph cannot provide a safe food identification. Do not consume a specimen based on this page.
